newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Soldier's death renews talk of N Ireland sniper.
newsitem.headline: Soldier's death renews talk of N Ireland sniper.

text.p: The IRA once put up a sign in the "bandit country" of south Armagh. Mimicking a British road sign, it said "Caution. Sniper at work."
The killing of a British soldier with a single high-velocity bullet on Wednesday night has raised fears the sniper is at work once again.

The sign showed a silhouetted Irish Republican Army (IRA) gunman in trademark balaclava and what looked like its traditional weapon, a Soviet-made AK-47 assault rifle. The bullet which slew 23-year-old Lance Bombardier Stephen Restorick was fired by a high-velocity rifle, probably from some distance and with fatal accuracy.

The woman the soldier was talking to at the time told reporters tearfully on Wednesday night that all she heard was a "crack" . The soldier slumped as he was handing her back her driving licence at an army checkpoint.

Security spokesmen declined to comment on the weapon used in the killing, which brought Northern Ireland back to the brink of renewed sectarian war between the IRA, which seeks to end British rule, and Protestant Loyalists who want to maintain it.

But security sources say that the IRA may have several high-powered sniping rifles acquired either through U.S. over- the-counter markets, where they are sold for hunting, or from some East European army arsenal through the black market.
They allow IRA killers to operate from long range in the hilly border area of south Armagh, which British soldiers call "bandit country" because of the cover it gives gunmen.

One rifle under suspicion is the American-made Barrett 0.5 calibre hunting rifle, which, with a telescopic sight, is deadly from up to a mile (two km). Its bullets are the size of machine gun rounds. If they hit home, the wound is usually fatal.
In the grisly folklore of Irish Republicanism, which sees the British army as legitimate targets and British rule as an illegal colonial throwback, the gun is called "The Terminator".

Security experts believe the IRA may have acquired a gas-operated East European V-94 rifle which can fire a round through a brick wall. It is accurate at half the distance of the Barrett but is equally lethal.
Bessbrook is Britain's army base in south Armagh and the busiest heliport in Europe because of army flights to supply and reinforce garrisons strung along the remote border area.
Its roads and lanes are too dangerous for motorised patrols because of snipers, landmines and concealed remotely-fired mortar bombs.
The soldier was shot at a permanent checkpoint outside the village where he was checking the papers of drivers.

Eyewtnesses said soldiers who arrived on the scene were visibly shocked. Security sources say that the fear of being in a sniper's sights is part of the IRA's constant psychological warfare against 18,000 British troops in the province.
Most IRA weaponry was acquired in the 1970s and 1980s, some of it from Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi who saw in the IRA an ally in his personal war against "Western Imperialism."

But a crackdown on smuggling by Britain and its Irish partners in the search for a lasting peace, together with tight surveillance of IRA fund-raising in the United States, severely curtailed the IRA's gun-running.

Security sources say there are persistent reports reaching them that the IRA did manage to smuggle in more arms, including snipers' rifles, in the mayhem that followed the collapse of the Berlin wall and, more recently, the break-up of Yugoslavia.
